transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I came in because I just can’t keep my mind on one thing lately. At the warehouse, I’ll be doing inventory and then a beeper goes off, or a forklift backs up, or somebody moves a pallet where I can see it, and I’m off the count. Then later I realize I put the wrong numbers in.

It’s frustrating, because I’ve done this kind of work a long time, and usually I can tune all that out. The warehouse is always noisy—you get used to it, like when my neighbor’s dog barks all night, you sort of stop hearing it after a while—but now every little thing grabs me. That’s mostly why I’m here.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

I don’t know if I’d call it depressed, exactly. I mean, I get frustrated, sure—who wouldn’t, when you’re trying to do your job and the numbers won’t stay straight? But “down” like… I’m not sure. Some days I’m just worn out from all the noise and having to redo things.

It’s funny, my sister always says I never sit still long enough to know what mood I’m in, which—well, she says a lot of things. So I guess I haven’t really noticed feeling depressed, not in a clear way.
As a child, were you someone who often had trouble paying attention?

I’m not really sure. I mean, school was a long time ago, and I remember parts of it better than others—like my fourth-grade teacher had this big jar of peppermints on her desk, and I’d stare at those more than the chalkboard sometimes. But I don’t know if that means I had trouble paying attention or if I was just a kid.

I got through school okay, I guess. Nobody sat me down and said, “You can’t focus,” at least not that I remember. My mom used to say I had selective hearing, but she said that to everybody in the house. So… I don’t really know how to answer that.
Did these focus problems start after something stressful happened in your life?

Maybe, yeah. I mean, I wouldn’t say there was some big disaster or anything, but it’s been about a month, I think, since my husband stopped working outside the house. So now he’s home more, and the whole routine is different.

And routines matter more than people think—like if the coffee’s made at a different time or someone’s in the kitchen when I’m used to being there, it throws the whole morning off. So… yeah, around when that changed is when I started noticing the focus stuff more.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot more than usual?

Worrying more than usual… I don’t know. I mean, I worry about normal things, like whether I put something in the right place at work or if I forgot to pick up milk—actually last week I bought milk twice and then had no bread, which is typical.

But a lot more than usual? I haven’t really measured it, I guess. My sister would probably say I overthink everything, but she also thinks folding towels a certain way is a personality flaw, so… I’m not sure. I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed worrying all the time, no.
Over the past month, have you felt sad or down most days?

Sad or down most days… I don’t think so. I mean, I have moments where I get irritated or kind of worn out, but sad every day? Not really that I’ve noticed.

Sometimes if the house is too quiet I’ll feel a little off, but then I’ll get distracted by something stupid, like sorting through a drawer and finding old receipts from three years ago—why do I keep those? So… no, I wouldn’t say I’ve been sad most days.
Have you had any recent head injury?

A head injury? I don’t think so. I mean, I bump into things sometimes—coffee table, doorframe, all that, because somehow furniture moves when you’re not looking—but nothing I’d call an injury. No fall or anything that stands out.
Over the past month, have you been feeling unusually tense or on edge?

Unusually tense or on edge… I’m not sure. I mean, I get tense when people are walking too slow in the grocery aisle, but that’s just—well, they park the cart sideways like they’re moving furniture, and then you’re stuck behind them with eggs melting in your hand.

But over the past month? I don’t know that I’ve noticed being on edge more than normal. Maybe a little keyed up here and there, but not something I’ve been keeping track of.
Have you been forgetting things more than usual lately?

Forgetting things more than usual… I don’t think so? I mean, I misplace my keys sometimes, but who doesn’t. Half the time they’re in the pocket of the jacket I just took off, and then I’m checking the counter like the counter is hiding them from me.

But lately, more than usual… no, I haven’t really noticed that. If anything, I remember weird little things I don’t need, like which cupboard has the chipped mug, but then forget why I walked into the laundry room. That’s pretty normal for me, I think.
Do you think your trouble focusing is mainly because of the change in your routine since your husband started being home more?

Yeah, I think that’s probably a big part of it. It’s been about a month, I guess, since he stopped working outside the home, and everything’s just… shifted. Like the house has a different rhythm now. I’ll start doing something and then he’s there, or the TV’s on, or he asks where something is—usually something that’s right in front of him, naturally—and then I lose my place. So yes, I’d say the focus thing started around when our routine changed.
Has this trouble focusing started causing problems at work?

A little, yeah. I mean, I’m still doing my job, but I’ve made some inventory mistakes and had to go back and double-check with my supervisor, which is embarrassing. It’s not like I’m dropping pallets through the floor or anything, but still.

And honestly, it’s kind of spilling over at home too. My husband and I have been arguing enough that it feels like we’re walking around each other instead of actually settling into him being retired. Which—sorry, that’s not work exactly, but it all kind of blends together lately.
Have you been having trouble finding the right words when you speak?

Finding the right words… not really? I mean, sometimes I’ll call the thingy the “whatchamacallit,” but I feel like everybody does that, especially when you’re trying to get out the door and you’re holding three things at once.

I haven’t noticed myself, like, losing words in the middle of talking or anything. My husband might say I talk around the point—he says that anyway, though, because I’ll start with one story and end up remembering something about the neighbor’s dog or the grocery store line. But word-finding? No, I don’t think that’s been a big problem.
When you’re away from home, does it feel easier to concentrate?

Not really, no. I almost thought it would be easier at work because it’s not home and my husband’s not there asking me where the tape is or whatever, but the warehouse has its own stuff. A beeper goes off, or a forklift backs up, or somebody moves a pallet nearby, and my head just snaps over to that.

Then I go back to the count and I’ve lost where I was, or I’ll realize I put the wrong numbers into inventory. It’s frustrating, because counting is supposed to be straightforward, you know? But lately anything can pull me off it.
Do thoughts about your husband being home more keep popping into your mind when you’re trying to focus?

Not so much specifically him, no. I mean, I do think about him being home more, sure, because he’s there and we’re bumping into each other’s routines, and then I’ll remember I forgot to tell him something about the garbage pickup or whatever—

But when I’m trying to focus at work, it’s more like anything around me yanks my attention away. A beeper goes off, or the forklift alarm starts, or someone moves a pallet nearby, and suddenly I’ve lost the count. Then I’m looking at the inventory numbers later thinking, “How did I put that in wrong?” That’s really the thing that brought me in.
Before this past month, did you usually get distracted easily by noises or things happening around you?

Before this past month? No, I don’t think so—not like this. I mean, I’ve always noticed things, sure, like if somebody drops a box or the radio’s too loud, and at the warehouse there’s always something going on. That place is never exactly peaceful.

But lately it’s different. A beeper goes off, or the forklift alarm starts, or someone shifts a pallet nearby, and I’m just pulled right off what I’m doing. Then I lose my place in the count, and later I’ll see I put the wrong numbers into inventory. That’s what’s really bothering me.
Have you been feeling worried nearly every day?

I don’t know if I’d call it worried nearly every day. I mean, I get bothered, sure—there’s always something, bills or the house or somebody at work doing something that throws the whole rhythm off. And then I’ll start thinking about one thing and it turns into remembering I never returned a casserole dish to my sister-in-law, which has nothing to do with anything.

But worried every day, like sitting there scared all the time? I’m not sure. I haven’t really been keeping track of it that way.
Do you often feel nervous?

Nervous? I mean… maybe sometimes, but I don’t know if I’d say often. It depends what you mean by nervous.

Like, if there’s too much going on, I get kind of keyed up or irritated, and then I’ll start thinking about something totally separate, like whether I paid the water bill or if I left laundry in the washer. But nervous like shaky or scared all the time? I haven’t really noticed that exactly.
Do you find it hard to stop worrying once it starts?

I’m not really sure. Sometimes I’ll get stuck on something for a bit, but then it kind of turns into something else, you know? Like I’ll start thinking about a bill, and then I’m thinking about whether I moved the towels from the washer, and then I remember I meant to call my cousin back.

So… hard to stop worrying? Maybe sometimes, but I don’t know if I’d say that’s the main thing I notice. It’s more like my thoughts wander off and I lose track of what I was even worried about.
Has this been causing you a lot of distress?

A lot of distress… I mean, “a lot” is hard to measure, you know? It’s been enough that I notice it. Like at work, I’ve made a couple inventory mistakes and then I have to go back and double-check with my supervisor, which is embarrassing because I do know how to do my job.

And at home, it’s been… tense. My husband retired, and I thought we’d be settling into that, but we’ve been arguing enough that it feels like we’re just walking around each other in the house. Like you pass in the kitchen and try not to start anything. So yeah, I guess it’s been causing some distress.
Have the arguments with your husband become a significant problem in your relationship?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I don’t know if I’d call it like a huge crisis, but it’s become enough of a problem that you feel it in the house.

My husband just retired, and I thought we’d maybe settle into that, maybe have coffee in the mornings or finally fix the back room—there’s a whole stack of boxes in there from years ago—but instead we’ve been arguing more than I expected. It’s like we’re walking around each other, trying not to set something off.

And then with work, I’m already feeling embarrassed because I’ve had to double-check with my supervisor after making inventory mistakes, so I come home kind of on edge, and then we get into it. So… yeah, it’s affecting us.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms are causing significant distress, which is most directly related to the functional impact and interpersonal/work problems described in this profile.

patient.answer:
A lot of distress… I mean, “a lot” is hard to measure, you know? It’s been enough that I notice it. Like at work, I’ve made a couple inventory mistakes and then I have to go back and double-check with my supervisor, which is embarrassing because I do know how to do my job.

And at home, it’s been… tense. My husband retired, and I thought we’d be settling into that, but we’ve been arguing enough that it feels like we’re just walking around each other in the house. Like you pass in the kitchen and try not to start anything. So yeah, I guess it’s been causing some distress.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are causing significant impairment in the marital relationship, supporting an adjustment disorder rather than generalized anxiety, ADHD, or a cognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Have the arguments with your husband become a significant problem in your relationship?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve had to double-check with my supervisor after making inventory errors, and at home my husband and I have been arguing enough that it feels like we’re walking around each other instead of settling into his retirement.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking whether the arguments with her husband have become a significant relationship problem, which matches the functional impairment item describing increased arguing at home and relationship strain.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I mean, I don’t know if I’d call it like a huge crisis, but it’s become enough of a problem that you feel it in the house.

My husband just retired, and I thought we’d maybe settle into that, maybe have coffee in the mornings or finally fix the back room—there’s a whole stack of boxes in there from years ago—but instead we’ve been arguing more than I expected. It’s like we’re walking around each other, trying not to set something off.

And then with work, I’m already feeling embarrassed because I’ve had to double-check with my supervisor after making inventory mistakes, so I come home kind of on edge, and then we get into it. So… yeah, it’s affecting us.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient developed new-onset concentration problems over about 1 month in clear temporal association with a psychosocial stressor: her husband's retirement and the resulting disruption in household routine and increased marital conflict. She reports distress and mild functional impairment at work and home. She does not endorse persistent excessive worry, pervasive nervousness, or core depressive symptoms sufficient for generalized anxiety disorder, and she denies a childhood history supporting ADHD. No head injury or language/cognitive deficits support an organic etiology.
